evidence_set: The review lists time since last administration among determinants of blood morphine, reports deaths occurring hours after administration, and cites three publications in support of possible overlap with survivors without giving numerical survivor-comparison details. It argues that multiple-drug toxicity may better describe many deaths. Editors' appraisal: co-detection does not quantify causal contributions; timing and unmeasured tolerance limit concentration comparisons. The review does not discuss post-mortem redistribution or specimen-site explanations, so these must not be attributed to its authors. The Michigan comparison cites Monforte 1977; 1977 is the publication year, not a reported case-collection period. Separately, the polydrug section says 12% of fatalities in Monforte were positive for diazepam; this is diazepam-specific detection, not evidence that diazepam was the only substance or only benzodiazepine detected. Whole-group benzodiazepine detection is reported as 55%, 27% and 22% in three other cited sources. These are the review's secondary reports; the cited primary studies were not independently read.

The sample comprises 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths reported to NP-SAD in England and Wales for 2000. Cases with insufficient information or the specified intentional/no-verdict exclusions were removed. Two researchers independently identified/classified cases, with confirmation by an addiction specialist. Direct overdose was assigned where no evidence suggested another cause. Counts were 802 direct overdose and 235 in other categories: 74 acute physical events, 40 non-drug-related medical conditions plus 72 drug-related medical conditions (112 combined), 31 traumatic accidents and 18 acute infections. Editors' calculations: 802/1,037=77.3% and 235/1,037=22.7%. The default can place unrecognized alternatives in direct overdose; treating those shares as a ceiling/floor is conditional on the other category assignments being correct, not a validated bound on true causes, a misclassification estimate or a comparison with official statistics. Table 2 prints methadone implicated in 107/802 direct-overdose deaths (13% printed; editors' exact calculation 13.34%), not 101/802. The separate text's 4% sole implication does not establish sole detection. Reporting was voluntary, and negative toxicology findings were not recorded, leaving absence versus non-testing uncertain.

evidence_set: Tables I-III label analytical amounts as mg/L plasma. Table I's fatal MDMA entries are 0.36, detected, detected in blood/urine, 0.424, a scan entry appearing as '0 11', 1.16 and 1.26. The conventional reading of the unclear entry is 0.11, giving five numerical readings spanning 0.11-1.26, but its decimal dot is not visible in this supplied scan. Table II's five people who survived severe complications have readings conventionally transcribed as 0.2, 0.7, 0.97, 0.24 and 0.21; the first two appear as '0 2' and '0 7' with missing/faint decimal dots. One is a 1-year-old child's accidental exposure. Table III's three people who survived road accidents have MDMA 0.05, 0.34 and 0.15; the two people who died have 0.10 and 0.13. Conditional on those conventional decimal readings, the eight survivor values range 0.05-0.97, all five severe-case values lie within the five-value fatal range, and the road-death value 0.10 lies below 0.11 while 0.13 lies within. The decimal uncertainty remains unresolved by another source. These are selected clinical/accident cases; sampling times and collection circumstances for each measurement are not reported, and the Results describes samples from road-accident scenes. The plasma headers do not establish that every value was collected in hospital or from femoral autopsy blood. These comparisons do not supply a healthy ordinary-use baseline or a validated fatal cutoff.
